Chapter 4: Removing Barriers—Creating Space and Focus for Practice.
Even when you’ve got a clear plan and a real desire to learn, sticking with it can still be tough. What usually gets in the way? Well, it’s rarely about skill or knowledge. More often, it’s the environment around you and the thoughts in your head that slow you down. Distractions, feeling short on time, or just worrying about looking silly—all of these can throw you off track. If you want to make the most of your first 20 hours, overcoming these barriers is absolutely essential.
So, where do you start? The first step is setting up a space that makes practice easy and focused. Think about it—how much more likely are you to stick with something if it’s right in front of you, and nothing’s pulling your attention away? Try carving out a dedicated spot for practice. Make it a phone-free, TV-free zone.
Next, put your learning time on the calendar—just like you would any important appointment. And get your materials ready ahead of time. That way, when it’s time to practice, you’re not scrambling to find what you need. These small changes send a clear message to your brain: learning matters. They cut down on excuses and make it so much easier to dive in.
But let’s be honest—sometimes the biggest hurdle isn’t your environment. It’s that uneasy feeling of being new at something. For a lot of adults, the thought of being a beginner again is just plain uncomfortable. You might worry about looking awkward, or get frustrated when things don’t click right away. The truth? That’s a totally normal part of learning.
Here’s something to remember: feeling clumsy is actually a sign you’re growing. Every expert started out as a beginner. Those first awkward steps—they’re supposed to feel hard. If you can accept that discomfort as just part of the journey, it gets a lot easier to keep going, even when it’s tough.
Time management is another big piece of the puzzle. Maybe you’ve told yourself you just don’t have enough time to pick up something new. But what if you could make progress, even with just a little time here and there? The key is consistency. Twenty hours of focused practice—spread out over days or weeks—can really add up. The trick is making learning a habit, not just something you do once in a while.
Here are a few simple strategies to keep you moving forward:
- Use a timer for short, focused sessions.
- Track your progress, so you can actually see how far you’ve come.
- And, if you can, find a buddy or a group to learn with. A little support and accountability go a long way.
The bottom line? When you tackle both the physical and emotional barriers to practice, you make space for real progress. Suddenly, it’s not about what’s holding you back—it’s about how much you can achieve with steady, focused effort.
